What is distance?
column2: The total length of the actual path traveled between two points (scalar — no direction).

column1: What is displacement?
column2: The length of the straight line between the starting and ending points, including direction (vector).

column1: Is distance dependent or independent of the path taken?
column2: Dependent — different paths between the same two points can have different distances.

column1: Is displacement dependent or independent of the path taken?
column2: Independent — displacement only depends on the start and end points, not the path.

column1: What does the symbol Δx represent?
column2: Displacement: Δx = x − x₀ (final position minus initial position).

column1: What does x₀ represent in class notation?
column2: Initial position.

column1: What does x (without a subscript) represent in class notation?
column2: Final position.

column1: Name the 5 vector quantities listed in class.
column2: Displacement, Velocity, Acceleration, Momentum, Force.

column1: Name the 5 scalar quantities listed in class.
column2: Distance, Speed, Time, Mass, Energy.

column1: Class example: a person starts at the 2 m mark, walks to the 8 m mark, then runs back to the -2 m mark. What is the TOTAL DISTANCE traveled?
column2: 16 m (6 m walk + 10 m run).

column1: Same example — what is the TOTAL DISPLACEMENT?
column2: -4 m, i.e. 4 m backward (from +2 m to -2 m).

column1: Same example — what is the displacement of just the walk (2 m → 8 m)?
column2: +6 m forward.

column1: Same example — what is the displacement of just the run (8 m → -2 m)?
column2: -10 m (10 m backward).

column1: Why can total distance be much larger than the magnitude of total displacement?
column2: Because distance adds up every bit of path length including backtracking, while displacement only reflects the net straight-line change from start to end.

column1: What is the formula for average velocity?
column2: v = Δx / t (displacement divided by the time interval).

column1: Is speed a scalar or a vector?
column2: Scalar — magnitude only, no direction.

column1: Is velocity a scalar or a vector?
column2: Vector — has both magnitude (speed) and direction.

column1: How is the symbol for velocity written differently from the symbol for speed?
column2: Speed = v (plain); Velocity = v (bold) or v with an arrow over it, since it's a vector.

column1: What are the standard units for speed/velocity used in this class?
column2: Meters per second (m/s).

column1: If you start at the zero mark and move in only one direction, how do distance and displacement compare?
column2: They are equal in magnitude — there's no backtracking to cause a difference.

column1: What's the difference between average velocity and instantaneous velocity?
column2: Average velocity = displacement over a longer time interval; instantaneous velocity = displacement during a tiny instant of time. Both include direction.

column1: Does a speedometer measure average speed, instantaneous speed, or velocity?
column2: Instantaneous speed — it shows the current rate of motion with no direction.

column1: LA driving scenario: speedometer reads 70 mph early, then 30 mph in traffic, never outside that range. Why isn't the trip's average velocity simply (70+30)/2?
column2: Average velocity = total displacement ÷ total time — it depends on how LONG you spent at each speed, not just the two extreme readings.

column1: If a leopard veers left but keeps the same speed, does its velocity change? Why?
column2: Yes — velocity includes direction, and the direction changed even though the speed (magnitude) didn't.

column1: Changes in velocity can come from what three things?
column2: A change in speed, a change in direction, or both.
